L213: # Compression as Adaptation: Implicit Visual Representation with Diffusion Foundation Models
L214: 
L215: This is the official code repository for the paper
L216: 
L217: cite89†Compression as Adaptation: Implicit Visual Representation with Diffusion Foundation Models†arxiv.org .
L218: 
L219: University of Cambridge, Microsoft Research Asia
L220: ## TL;DR
L221: 
L222: A single vector (1x131072) is enough to represent a 480p, 81-frame video!
L223: 
L224: ## Visual Results
L225: 
L226: ### Video Compression
L227: 
L228: 480p video compression at 11.8KB/s (30fps).
L229: 
L230: Ground Truth | VOV (Ours)
L231: 
L232: ### Beyond Compression: Editing
L233: 
L234: Native video editing with T2V model.
L235: 
L236: Original | Edited
L237: 
L238: > For more visual results and interactive demos, visit our cite90†project page†compressionasadaptation.github.io .
L239: ## Abstract
L240: Modern visual generative models acquire rich visual knowledge through large-scale training, yet existing visual representations (such as pixels, latents, or tokens) remain external to the model and cannot directly exploit this knowledge for compact storage or reuse. In this work, we introduce a new visual representation framework that encodes a signal as a function, which is parametrized by low-rank adaptations attached to a frozen visual generative model.
L241: Such implicit representations of visual signals, e.g., an 81-frame video, can further be hashed into a single compact vector, achieving strong perceptual video compression at extremely low bitrates. Beyond basic compression, the functional nature of this representation enables inference-time scaling and control, allowing additional refinement on the compression performance.
L242: More broadly, as the implicit representations directly act as a function of the generation process, this suggests a unified framework bridging visual compression and generation.
L243: ## Code Structure
L244: 
L245:     `VisionAsAdaptations/
L246:     ├── image/                          # Image pipeline (Qwen-Image)
L247:     │   ├── train_lora_multi.py         # Multi-GPU LoRA training
L248:     │   ├── reconstruct_lora_multi.py   # Reconstruction from LoRA weights
L249:     │   ├── config_train.py             # Training argument parser
L250:     │   ├── data_utils.py               # Data loading & preprocessing
L251:     │   ├── unilora_utils.py            # LoRA injection helpers
L252:     │   ├── pipelines/                  # Qwen-Image diffusion pipeline
L253:     │   ├── unilora/                    # UniLoRA layer & model implementation
L254:     │   └── descriptions/               # Image caption files
L255:     │
L256:     └── video/                          # Video pipeline (Wan2.1)
L257:         ├── train/                      # Two-stage training
L258:         │   ├── stage1_vm/              #   Stage 1: Visual-Memory style overfitting
L259:         │   └── stage2_vs/              #   Stage 2: Rate-distortion with entropy term
L260:         ├── scaling/                    # Inference-time scaling reconstruction
L261:         ├── edit/                       # Caption editing & LoRA merging
L262:         └── eval/                       # Evaluation (PSNR, DISTS, LPIPS, FVD)
L263:     `
L264: Each subdirectory contains its own `README.md` with detailed environment setup and usage instructions.
L265: ## Getting Started
L266: ### Image Pipeline
L267: 
L268:     cd image
L269:     pip install -r requirements.txt
L270: 
L271:     # Training (multi-GPU)
L272:     DATA_ROOT=/path/to/images \
L273:     CACHE_DIR=/path/to/pretrained_models \
L274:     bash train_multi.sh
L275: 
L276:     # Reconstruction
L277:     INIT_LORA_PATH=/path/to/lora_checkpoint.safetensors \
L278:     DATA_ROOT=/path/to/images \
L279:     CACHE_DIR=/path/to/pretrained_models \
L280:     bash reconstruct_multi.sh
L281: See cite91†`image/README.md` for full details on environment variables (`NUM_GPUS`, `OUT_DIR`, `DESCRIPTION_FILE`, `WIDTH`, `HEIGHT`, etc.).
L282: ### Video Pipeline
L283: 
L284:     cd video
L285:     pip install -r requirements.txt
L286: Training (two-stage):
L287: 
L288:     cd train
L289: 
L290:     # Stage 1 — Visual-Memory style single-video overfitting
L291:     FRAMES_DIR=/path/to/frames \
L292:     CAPTION_FILE=/path/to/caption.txt \
L293:     CACHE_DIR=/path/to/pretrained_models \
L294:     bash stage1_train.sh
L295: 
L296:     # Stage 2 — Rate-distortion with entropy coding
L297:     INIT_LORA_PATH=/path/to/stage1_checkpoint.safetensors \
L298:     FRAMES_DIR=/path/to/frames \
L299:     CAPTION_FILE=/path/to/caption.txt \
L300:     CACHE_DIR=/path/to/pretrained_models \
L301:     bash stage2_train.sh
L302:     # Or run both stages sequentially
L303:     bash run_two_stage.sh
L304: Inference-time scaling:
L305: 
L306:     cd scaling
L307:     bash sample.sh
L308: 
L309: Editing (caption change or LoRA merge):
L310: 
L311:     cd edit
L312:     # Same LoRA, new caption
L313:     WEIGHTS=/path/to/lora.safetensors CAPTION="new prompt" bash edit_caption.sh
L314: 
L315:     # Merge two LoRAs
L316:     WEIGHTS1=/path/to/lora1.safetensors WEIGHTS2=/path/to/lora2.safetensors \
L317:     CAPTION="new prompt" bash edit_merge.sh
L318: 
L319: Evaluation:
L320: 
L321:     cd eval
L322:     bash eval.sh
L323: See cite92†`video/README.md` and each subfolder's README for full configuration options.

L21@P0: 1. Introduction
L22@P0: Large-scale visual generative models (Esser et al., 2024;
L23@P0: Brooks et al., 2024) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in synthesizing and manipulating visual content by
L24@P0: learning rich visual knowledge from massive data. With the
L25@P0: progression from image to video synthesis, these models
L26@P0: are further expected to leverage such visual knowledge for
L27@P0: higher-level visual reasoning (Wiedemer et al., 2025), moving toward unified and generalist vision foundation models.
L28@P0: Despite this rich visual knowledge embedded in visual gen-

L37@P0: (Meng et al., 2022), latent variables (Rombach et al., 2022)
L38@P0: or tokens (Esser et al., 2021), which must be separately
L39@P0: encoded and then fed into the model to enable downstream
L40@P0: interactions such as editing. This separation between internal model knowledge and external signal representations
L41@P0: may lead to redundancy and inefficiency in representation,
L42@P0: and limits the ability of the generative model to store or
L43@P0: reuse past visual information over time.
L44@P0: To address this gap, we explore encoding visual signals as
L45@P0: a function that describes the generation process, enabling
L46@P0: synergy with large-scale generative models. This method—
L47@P0: representing signals as a function rather than an explicit
L48@P0: array—is commonly referred to as implicit (or functional)
L49@P0: representations. An example is the implicit neural representations (INR). They model visual signals as continuous coordinate-based functions, typically parameterized by
L50@P0: small multi-layer perceptrons (Mildenhall et al., 2021; Sitzmann et al., 2020). While effective in compressing individual signals (Dupont et al., 2021), they are trained largely
L51@P0: from scratch and remain decoupled from the rich knowledge
L52@P0: learned by large-scale models across diverse data.
L53@P0: In this work, we propose to compress visual signals as model
L54@P0: adaptations to large-scale diffusion generative models via
L55@P0: parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques (Mangrulkar et al., 2022), such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA)
L56@P0: (Hu et al., 2022). While LoRA has been widely used for
L57@P0: tasks like personalized generation (Ruiz et al., 2023; Kumari
L58@P0: et al., 2023), we show that it also encodes implicit representations when optimized for specific visual content. Leveraging the pretrained generative model as a visual knowledge
L59@P0: prior, such implicit representations emphasize high-level
L60@P0: visual semantics, making it particularly effective for compression. Moreover, we show that the induced adaptation
L61@P0: parameters can be mapped into a single compact vector (Li
L62@P0: et al., 2025), enabling compression of visual signals (such
L63@P0: as an 81-frame video) into one vector.
L64@P0: We demonstrate that such implicit visual representations
L65@P0: achieve strong perceptual video compression performance at

L136@P1: control, allowing quality improvement through inferencetime scaling. More broadly, the functional representations
L137@P1: can be used beyond the reconstruction task and can serve as
L138@P1: “visual memories” on specific identities, acting during the
L139@P1: generation process, which suggests a step towards a unified
L140@P1: framework to bridge compression and adaptive generation
L141@P1: within pretrained generative foundation models.
L142@P1: In short, our core contributions include:
L143@P1: • We describe a framework that represents a visual signal
L144@P1: as a function that generates the signal. Such implicit
L145@P1: representations naturally leverage the rich knowledge
L146@P1: embedded in large-scale visual generative models.
L147@P1: • We propose an approach that compresses the function
L148@P1: into a single adaptation vector, achieving strong perceptual compression results on videos.
L149@P1: • We identify a key advantage of the functional representations: they can be flexibly controlled at inference
L150@P1: time. Based on this insight, we introduce an inferencetime scaling strategy for compression, which significantly improves reconstruction fidelity.
L151@P1: 2. Background
L152@P1: 2.1. Explicit and Implicit Representations
L153@P1: The distinction between explicit and implicit representations
L154@P1: varies across research contexts. In some works such as
L155@P1: implicit chain-of-thoughts (Deng et al., 2024; Zhu et al.,
L156@P1: 2025), latent activations from neural networks are regarded
L157@P1: as implicit representations, emphasizing their lack of direct
L158@P1: interpretability. In contrast, much of the visual compression
L159@P1: literature adopts a different perspective, where the distinction is defined by how signal information is represented:
L160@P1: whether it is explicitly exposed as symbolic variables or
L161@P1: implicitly encoded within a parametrized function (Dupont
L162@P1: et al., 2021). In this paper, we follow the latter convention,
L163@P1: where pixels, tokens, and latent variables are all treated as
L164@P1: explicit representations.
L165@P1: Explicit representations for visual compression Traditional lossy visual compression methods rely on explicit
L166@P1: latent representations. A visual signal is encoded into a
L167@P1: compact latent code, and reconstructed through a shared decoder. In this formulation, all sample-specific information
L168@P1: is stored in the latent code, while the decoder remains fixed
L169@P1: across signals. This paradigm underlies neural codecs (Balle´
L170@P1: et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; Guo et al.,
L171@P1: 2021) based on variational autoencoders (VAEs) (Kingma
L172@P1: & Welling, 2014), where compression performance is governed by the expressiveness and entropy of the latent space.
L173@P1: Implicit representations as functions In this work, we
L174@P1: use the term implicit representation to mean a functional encoding of a sample, i.e., representing a sample as a function.
L175@P1: The function inputs could be coordinates (Stanley, 2007)
L176@P1: or noise, which are shared or signal-agnostic, without any
L177@P1: semantic information about the signal itself. Figure 1a and
L178@P1: 1b illustrate such differences.
L179@P1: One specific example of the implicit representation is implicit neural representation (INR), which parametrizes the
L180@P1: function with a small neural network. Such INRs enable
L181@P1: compact and continuous representations of images (Dupont
L182@P1: et al., 2021), videos (Chen et al., 2021), and 3D scenes
L183@P1-2: (Mildenhall et al., 2021), which have motivated recent ex2Compression as Adaptation: Implicit Visual Representation with Diffusion Foundation Models
L184@P2: ploration of INRs for visual compression. However, existing
L185@P2: INR-based compression methods (Guo et al., 2023; He et al.,
L186@P2: 2024a; Kwan et al., 2024) typically rely on small standalone
L187@P2: networks, limiting their ability to recognize or exploit the
L188@P2: rich visual knowledge, even in some recent works where
L189@P2: INRs are trained with diffusion process (Gao et al., 2025b).
L190@P2: 2.2. Diffusions and Flows
L191@P2: Our method builds on diffusion- and flow-based large-scale
L192@P2: visual generative models (Wan et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025).
L193@P2: A diffusion model (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021) specifies a forward stochastic differential equation (SDE), gradually corrupting data to noise. We learn a score function by
L194@P2: denoising score matching (DSM, Vincent, 2011) to reverse
L195@P2: the noising process, mapping noise back to data.
L196@P2: Many recent vision models (Wan et al., 2025; Wu et al.,
L197@P2: 2025) are instead trained under a flow matching formulation
L198@P2: (Lipman et al., 2023). The model learns a time-dependent
L199@P2: vector field v(xt, t) and generates samples by solving an
L200@P2: ordinary differential equation (ODE) defined by the vector
L201@P2: field. With the common flow-matching formulation, the flow
L202@P2: ODE admits an equivalent diffusion variant that preserves
L203@P2: the same marginal densities, and the vector field can be
L204@P2: directly related to the score. We detail the connection and
L205@P2: the conversion between these formulations in Section C.3.
L206@P2: For the diffusion and flow-based vision foundation model,
L207@P2: the generative procedure starts from random noise and then
L208@P2: evolves the sample following the denoising SDE or the ODE.
L209@P2: The samples they generated are determined by the entire
L210@P2: dynamics, and hence, the generation process can be viewed
L211@P2: as a representation of the generated sample.
L212@P2: 3. Methods
L213@P2: This section presents our methods in details. We will begin with a high-level motivation and introduction to the
L214@P2: framework of implicit visual representations.
L215@P2: 3.1. Learning Implicit Visual Representations
L216@P2: Motivations Our method starts from a simple observation:
L217@P2: modern diffusion foundation models already contain a large
L218@P2: amount of reusable visual knowledge in their weights, and
L219@P2: they express this knowledge through a generation process.
L220@P2: Strong priors about what “natural” images or videos look
L221@P2: like are encoded in the pretrained weights and expressed
L222@P2: through the entire generative procedure. Therefore, instead
L223@P2: of compressing what the visual signal is, we compress how
L224@P2: to generate the visual signal. In other words, rather than
L225@P2: representing a visual sample explicitly (as pixels, latents, or
L226@P2: tokens), we seek implicit visual representation as specified
L227@P2: generation functions defined on top of the foundation model.
